The Rusty-breasted Antpitta Grallaricula ferrugineipectus is a small passerine inhabiting the understory of montane cloud forests in South America. Clutch size consistently consists of two eggs per nest [N_R_i = two eggs per nest], and field observations indicate that breeding pairs raise a single brood each year [F_R_i = a single brood each year], a reproductive schedule that aligns with the limited productivity typical of many Neotropical insectivores. During the initial stages of post-hatching development, nestlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 2.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.3 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the altricial condition of the hatchlings. Over the subsequent days, the chick undergoes rapid mass accumulation. When maintained under stable incubation conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth is 17 days [ab = 17 days], which corresponds to the incubation period required for the embryo to complete organogenesis and pipping. This value falls within the range of 16 to 17.5 days reported across the species' geographic distribution, attesting to the consistency of the developmental program despite local climatic variation.

An additional perspective on early ontogeny involves the freshly laid egg, which provides an estimate of initial wet weight at oviposition. Data collected from a series of nests in the eastern Andes indicate that the initial wet weight of a newly deposited egg, measured before the onset of embryonic development, averages 2.78 grams [Ww0 = 2.78 grams]. This measurement aligns with the egg mass required to provision a developing embryo through the incubation period. Recorded values range from 2.4 to approximately 3.02 grams, with the variation likely linked to maternal condition and territory quality. This investment in egg mass is noteworthy given that females themselves reach an ultimate wet weight of 16.48 grams [Wwi = 16.48 grams] at adulthood. The ratio of egg mass to adult female mass, at roughly 17 percent, is moderately high for a bird of this size and suggests the species directs considerable resources into each offspring. Such a pattern is typical of tropical passerines that produce few eggs per year.

Observations suggest that fledglings quickly develop the foraging skills necessary to capture arthropod prey in the leaf litter, though they remain vulnerable during this post-fledgling stage.
